tc_fork_desc: One piece attacks two or more at once. The opponent can save only one — you take the other.
tc_pin_desc: A piece can't leave the line because the king or a more valuable piece stands behind it. Pile up on the pinned piece.
tc_skewer_desc: A pin in reverse: attack the valuable piece, it steps aside and exposes the one behind it.
tc_doubleAttack_desc: Two threats in one move — by a fork or by opening a line. The opponent can't parry both.
tc_discoveredAttack_desc: One piece moves off a line and unmasks another's attack, while making a threat of its own.
tc_deflection_desc: Force a defender away from a key square or line, and what it guarded is left hanging.
tc_attraction_desc: A sacrifice lures an enemy piece, often the king, onto a bad square where a blow is waiting.
tc_intermezzo_desc: Instead of the expected reply, first a forcing in-between move, often a check, then the recapture.
tc_sacrifice_desc: Give up material for something bigger: an attack on the king, mate, or winning even more back.
tc_hangingPiece_desc: An enemy piece is attacked and undefended. Spotting and taking it is the first tactical skill.
tc_promotion_desc: A pawn reaches the last rank and becomes a queen — often with the help of a sacrifice or a deflection.
tc_backRankMate_desc: The king is boxed in by its own pawns on the back rank — a rook or queen mates along it.
tc_mateIn1_desc: Find the move that leaves the king no escape.
tc_mateIn2_desc: Forced mate in two: the first move cages the king or gains the tempo for the final blow.
tc_mateIn3_desc: A short forced combination of three moves. Calculate to the end — every reply of the opponent.
op_italian_idea: White develops the bishop to c4 against the weak f7 square, castles and prepares d4 with a quiet c3 — the classic open game.
op_ruy-lopez_idea: The bishop on b5 pressures the c6 knight, defender of e5. White plays for lasting central pressure — the deepest open game.
op_scotch_idea: White opens the centre at once with d4 and trades on c6, saddling Black with doubled pawns — clear, active play.
op_kings-gambit_idea: White gives up the f-pawn for quick development and the open f-file against the king. Sharp 19th-century romance.
op_london_idea: One solid setup against almost anything: d4, Bf4, e3, c3 — a firm centre without memorising lines.
op_english_idea: White grips the centre from the flank with c4 and fianchettoes the bishop on g2 — a Sicilian with an extra tempo.
op_petrov_idea: Black answers symmetrically and attacks e4 in turn. A solid defence where copying White blindly is punished.
op_najdorf_idea: The move a6 prepares queenside play and e5 in the centre. The sharpest, most studied Sicilian.
op_dragon_idea: The g7 bishop breathes down the long diagonal like a dragon. Opposite-side attacks — whoever is faster wins.
op_french_idea: Black builds the e6–d5 chain and undermines White's centre with c5 and f6. Patient counterplay.
op_caro-kann_idea: Like the French, but the c8 bishop gets out before e6. A sturdy structure with few weaknesses.
op_scandinavian_idea: Black hits e4 at once and brings the queen out early, tucking it on a5 — simple, clear play.
op_pirc_idea: Black cedes the centre to strike at it later: fianchetto, d6 and a counter-blow on White's pawns.
op_qga_idea: Black takes on c4 but doesn't cling to the pawn, developing fast and hitting the centre with c5.
op_qgd_idea: Black holds d5 with e6 and develops calmly. The classic reliable defence.
op_slav_idea: Black defends d5 with c6 and keeps the c8 bishop free. Solid without being passive.
op_queens-indian_idea: Black controls e4 with pieces, not pawns — a b7 fianchetto or the bishop sortie to a6.
op_kings-indian_idea: Black cedes the centre, castles behind the g7 bishop, strikes with e5 and storms the kingside.
op_nimzo-indian_idea: The Bb4 pin stops e4. Black is ready to give the bishop for the knight to damage White's pawns.
op_dutch_idea: The f5 move grabs e4 and prepares a kingside attack. In the Stonewall the d5–e6–f5 pawns form a wall.
